title: The Shirt-Collar

full_text:
There was once a fine gentleman whose entire wardrobe consisted of a single bootjack, a mustache-comb, and an extraordinary stiff white shirt-collar. The shirt-collar was proud beyond measure, believing himself the finest dandy in the world.

When he was sent to the wash-tub, he met a modest iron garter. "My word, what a slender waist!" declared the collar. "May I ask your name?" "I do not give my name to strangers," retorted the garter. "Ah, playing coy!" laughed the collar. "I am a gentleman who owns a bootjack and a comb!"

Next, he was placed on the ironing board before the hot flatiron. "Sweet widow with the burning heart!" exclaimed the collar. "You smooth my edges so tenderly; marry me!" The iron scorched him brown in anger and moved away.

Then came the scissors with sharp blades: "What an exquisite ballet dancer!" said the collar. "You stretch your legs so gracefully!" The scissors snapped: "You impertinent rag!" and snipped his ragged edges off.

Finally, worn and yellowed, the collar was cast into the rag-bag and sent to the paper mill.

In the vat, he was beaten, mashed, boiled, and pressed into a sheet of white paper upon which this very story was printed. Even as paper, he bragged to the other sheets that he had broken the hearts of hundreds of ladies, iron-widows, and dancing scissors—proving that a braggart remains a boaster even after he has been ground to pulp in the rag-mill.
moral: Boasting of imaginary conquests leads only to the paper mill of public ridicule.
